name: Honduras
summary_text: Nothing in Honduran law criminalises gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Honduras since 1899, with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.  The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance for criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights or refuses a professional service on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. The provisions were retained in the new Code after LGBTI rights groups met with Congress on the wording.  The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits arrest of anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals. LGBTI organizations have documented numerous instances in which police have used this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.  Human Rights Watch reported in May 2009 that police in Honduras subjected transgender people to rape, assault and extortion. International human rights organizations have stated that the military government targeted LGBTI people for harassment, abuse and murder.  Honduras holds transgender women in the men's penitentiary system, with no placement by gender identity policy. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the La Isla module beside the unit for mentally ill prisoners. Trans women there are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women and denied conjugal visits. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture prevention centre CPTRT was she separated from men and her belongings returned.  Human Rights Watch confirmed in 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of guards. The judge had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate.  Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. A 2005 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses recognition of same-sex marriages or unions legally performed in other countries under Article 112, and prohibits adoption by same-sex couples under Article 116. Same-sex couples lack the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.  Registered violence includes 69 transgender persons among 174 violent LGBTI deaths between 2009 and 2014, and 264 LGBTI people murdered between 2009 and 2017, concentrated in Cortes and Francisco Morazan. Transgender activist Cynthia Nicole was shot dead on 2 January, and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez was murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 Spain granted asylum to a transsexual woman from Honduras after a police officer attempted to assassinate her. Vicky Hernandez v. Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.  Impunity is structural. LGBTI persons, particularly trans women, face major obstacles to justice linked to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases. The United States Department of State 2021 Human Rights Report listed violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.  Official hostility is on record. President Juan Orlando Hernandez said on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he was personally against same-sex marriage. The president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws. The two major parties have largely ignored LGBTI rights.
